description: Stories are meant to be told
summary:
What the Void Kept? : 
An interactive website that tells the stories of eight machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space: the Apollo 11, 12 and 15 lunar modules, Surveyor 3, Pioneer 10, Voyager 1, the Kepler telescope and the Opportunity rover.

Each machine gets its own story, written in plain language for school-age students and built chapter by chapter from NASA records. Readers can scroll through a photo story made from real mission images, switch to a read-aloud card mode with a narrator, or walk across a 3D lunar landscape for Apollo 11.

The challenge asks for storytelling that brings this hardware to life. We wish to portray each one not merely as a piece of hardware, but as a character with a purpose, a struggle to endure, and a legacy to leave behind. Their stories deserve to be told, for they paved the way for the missions we celebrate today, yet their names and deeds remain hidden from the eyes of so many young dreamers. It is time, therefore, to turn these forgotten pioneers into stories worth remembering.
details:
What it does

The home page lists the machines by where they rest: the Moon, Mars and deep space. Each one opens a story with three ways to experience it:

- A scrolling photo story, with one real NASA image per chapter and a key fact beside it.

- A card mode for younger readers, with large text and a narrator that reads each card aloud.

- A 3D scene for Apollo 11, where you scroll across the Sea of Tranquility past painted cut-outs of the lander, the flag and the experiments, under a night sky with the Earth overhead.

Every story ends with what the machine left behind and a list of the NASA pages its facts came from.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission pages are written for adults and are dense with technical terms. Our stories keep the real figures but explain them with comparisons a child can picture, and ask the reader questions along the way. The aim is for a student to finish a story knowing what the machine was, why it was sent, what it found and why it still matters. Teachers can use the card mode in class, and the narrator helps readers who struggle with long text.

Tools

- Next.js, React and TypeScript for the site, with Tailwind CSS for styling.

- GSAP and Lenis for scroll-driven animation.

- three.js with custom shaders for the 3D lunar scene.

- Blender to build the lunar terrain, compressed so it loads quickly on phones.

- Python with OpenCV to cut subjects out of NASA photos and repaint them in a watercolour paper style.

- The browser's built-in speech for the narrator, so no audio files are needed.

- NASA sources: the Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, NASA Science mission pages, NASA news releases and the NASA Image and Video Library.

How it is creative

The machines are the main characters. The site uses real photographs wherever they exist and labels artist's paintings clearly. The 3D scene mixes a realistic Moon surface with hand-painted paper cut-outs, so it feels like a picture book you can walk through. Three colour themes let readers choose a look they like.

What we considered

- Accuracy: every fact was checked against NASA records, and where NASA pages disagree we use the wording both support.

- Reading level: short sentences, one idea per paragraph, units a child knows.

- Accessibility: narration, keyboard navigation, readable contrast, and a still version for people who turn off motion.

- Speed: the site works on phones, with a lighter 3D model for small screens.

- Honesty about images: only pictures from the mission itself, each credited with its NASA image ID.
